cues.text: Physicians Who Charged Nothing

Cosmas and Damian were twin brothers, born, by tradition, in Arabia and trained in the art of medicine, who established a considerable reputation practicing at the port city of Aegea in Cilicia, in what is now southern Turkey.
What set them apart from other physicians of their day was their refusal to accept any payment for their services.
This practice earned them the Greek title anargyroi — 'the silverless' — and won many patients to the Christian faith through their evident charity.
Faith Through Free Healing
Their reputation for compassionate, unpaid care spread widely across the region, earning the brothers trust among those they treated.
The brothers used this trust to quietly evangelize those they treated and their neighbors.
A considerable number of their patients and neighbors converted to Christianity in a still largely pagan corner of the empire.
Arrest Under Diocletian
When the persecution under Emperor Diocletian reached Cilicia, the local prefect Lysias had Cosmas and Damian arrested and commanded them to renounce their faith.

According to their traditional Acts, the brothers withstood repeated tortures — including exposure to water, fire, and being thrown from a cross — emerging each time miraculously unharmed, before finally being put to death by the sword.
A Family of Martyrs
Tradition holds that three of their own brothers — Anthimus, Leontius, and Euprepius — were martyred alongside them on the same day, traditionally dated to 27 September.
That day was probably in the year 287, making the account one of a whole Christian family's shared witness rather than the twins' alone.
Imperial and Papal Honor
Their remains were buried at Cyrus in Syria, a city the Byzantine emperor Justinian I later restored lavishly in their honor after crediting their intercession with curing him of a dangerous illness.
Likewise, in Constantinople, Justinian rebuilt and adorned a church dedicated to the twins.
In Rome, Pope Felix IV consecrated a church to them in the sixth century.
Its ancient mosaics remain among the most treasured surviving artworks of the early Roman Church.
Legacy

Cosmas and Damian became, and remain, the patron saints of physicians, surgeons, and the medical profession generally, honored by name in the Roman Canon of the Mass alongside the other ancient martyrs.
Their example of medicine offered freely, out of love rather than profit, has made them an enduring model for Catholic hospitals and medical charities down to the present day.
